subtype: Approach: all-or-nothing plan with a five-day-a-week gym [Pitfall]
passage:
1 January. Tanvir came home with a receipt for a year's gym membership and a schedule stuck to the fridge: five days a week, hard sessions, no excuses. His cousin Aparna raised an eyebrow. "Start smaller?" "No. Go big or nothing," he said.

19 January. Tanvir had caught a cold, and work was heavy that week. He missed three sessions. On the fridge, the days he'd crossed off had gaps, and the streak was gone. He told himself he could restart on Monday, then didn't.

3 February. The schedule was still on the fridge, but Tanvir had stopped looking at it. He told Aparna he'd "never been a gym person anyway," and pulled the membership card out of sight, feeling like he'd failed.

qa.q: What did Tanvir buy on 1 January?
How did Tanvir feel on 3 February when he put the membership card out of sight?
qa.a: Tanvir felt like a failure and avoided the reminder, hiding his disappointment behind a shrug.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do differently if he wants to restart, and why?
qa.a: Tanvir could plan two or three shorter sessions and allow for sick or busy weeks, because a plan that bends is likelier to survive than one that breaks.

qa.q: How might Aparna see Tanvir's plan from the beginning?
qa.a: Aparna raised an eyebrow on 1 January, so Aparna probably saw the plan as too big and now may see the disappointment as avoidable.

grounding: Motivated on 1 January, the person signs up for a year with hard daily workouts, then drops the whole plan after a cold and a busy week.

subtype: Approach: all-or-nothing plan with a five-day-a-week gym [Pitfall]
passage:
"Pema, I saw you signed up for a full year at the gym. Sit with me a minute, and let your old aunt Shalini tell you what I did at twenty-one.
The first of January. I was so fired up. I paid for a year and wrote a plan: five days a week, an hour of hard training every day, no rest weeks. I even stuck it on the mirror.
For two weeks it was glorious. Then I caught a bad cold. Then office audits came, late nights all week. I missed six days in a row.
And instead of starting again gently, I looked at that mirror plan and thought, I've ruined it. I'm just not a fitness person. I never went back. The membership card is still in a drawer somewhere.
The streak didn't break me. The all-or-nothing did. So tell me, beta, what will you do on the week you're sick?"

qa.q: How many days in a row did Shalini miss?
qa.a: She missed six days in a row.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel after missing six days?
qa.a: Shalini felt like a failure, thinking she had ruined the plan and wasn't a fitness person at all.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Shalini's story, and what could have changed it?
qa.a: The turning point was deciding the plan was ruined after six missed days; restarting gently with a smaller routine would have kept the habit alive.

qa.q: How might the young Shalini have felt looking at the mirror plan that week?
qa.a: She likely felt ashamed and defeated, with the strict plan on the mirror reminding her of every missed day.

grounding: Shows a person starting a year-long, daily hard-workout plan on 1 January and dropping it entirely after a cold and a busy week.

subtype: Approach: all-or-nothing plan with a five-day-a-week gym [Pitfall]
passage:
Disha walked into the new year with a gym membership for twelve months and a spreadsheet: Monday to Friday, ninety minutes each, weights and cardio, no excuses. Her flatmate Sunaina raised an eyebrow. "Every day?"
"Every day. Half-measures don't work for me."
The first two weeks went perfectly. Then the monsoon arrived early in their coastal town, the roads flooded, and the gym's power went out three evenings in a row. The same week her office had a product launch, and she got home past ten every night. By Friday she had a streaming cold.
She looked at the spreadsheet: five red crosses in a row. She closed the laptop. "That's it. I'm done. I obviously can't do this."
She didn't go back in February. When Sunaina suggested a short walk on the terrace, Disha just shook her head.

qa.q: How long was each of Disha's planned gym sessions?
qa.a: Each session was planned for ninety minutes.

qa.q: How did Disha feel seeing five red crosses on the spreadsheet?
qa.a: She felt defeated and like a failure, deciding she obviously couldn't do it and closing the laptop.

qa.q: What approach would have suited Disha better during the flood week?
qa.a: A flexible plan with a small home version, like a terrace walk or ten minutes of stretching, would have kept the habit going when the gym was out.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Disha refuses the terrace walk?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel sad and a bit helpless, watching her friend give up the whole thing over one bad week.

grounding: Shows a person starting an all-or-nothing daily gym plan, then abandoning it entirely after weather, work and a cold break the streak.
